entry.title: For students: a source that cites itself, survives, and can be read by a machine
entry.summary: Three things go wrong with a web source in a term paper: it disappears, its citation is missing, and the file is unreadable for a language model. What a full-page capture does about each — with the measurements, including where it fails.

entry.title: I installed my own tool as a stranger would. Four things were wrong.
entry.summary: The install instructions were tested — by the author, on the machine where everything was already present. A clean install on the same computer found a setup window no script can click, a documented measurement that applied to nobody, an exception on every window message, and two unstated assumptions.

entry.title: Nineteen issues, and the two that mattered were about our own mistakes
entry.summary: Twelve closed, seven open. The valuable ones were not features: a published comparison that understated our own tool for two days, a hardcoded version that let the Chrome build fall fifteen releases behind, and a checksum that nearly started hashing an empty field. What a project looks like when the checks find more than the people do.

entry.title: How an AI agent turns a web page into a citable PDF
entry.summary: An agent asked to cite a source meets a paywall, a login or a page built by script, and an anonymous fetch returns nothing citable — 10 of 20 sources in our own test. Measured 4 August 2026: installing the capture extension takes 0.12 s in Firefox and 5.49 s in Chrome, with no window and no input event, and removing it is the same route backwards. What that gives an agent, what it does not, and the mistake that kept it hidden.

entry.title: An agent can install an extension in both browsers. Whether it may is a different question
entry.summary: Measured 4 August 2026: Firefox in 5.2 s over Marionette, Chrome in 10.7 s over an external extension marker that makes Chrome fetch the store build itself. No window, no click, no administrator rights — the browser only has to belong to the agent. What that changes for an extension, and where consent stops being a technical question.

entry.title: A capture at 8.5 % of the size, and OCR reads it slightly better
entry.summary: Measured 4 August 2026: on a text page, black and white cuts the file to 8.5 % of the current JPEG while Tesseract reads back 989 words against 987 in colour. Built into 2.28.0 as a setting, not a default — on a page with photographs the same setting falls apart.

entry.title: Who actually reads this site: 24 hours of crawler logs, published
entry.summary: AI systems made more requests to this site than search engines did — 299 against 282 in 24 hours, on a domain two days old. ClaudeBot and GPTBot lead. Twenty requests carrying AI user agents were not reading at all but scanning for /keys.json and /.git/HEAD, and are counted separately. Self-reported figures with the query published.

entry.title: Where citation data actually lives: 18 scholarly platforms measured
entry.summary: Which platforms declare citation data a reader can use? Eleven of eighteen returned a record, ten of them complete. The most complete record of all came from the DOI resolver — not from the article page. Mit deutscher Fassung.

entry.title: Twenty links, ten citations: what a machine finishes and what it hands back
entry.summary: Turning a reading list into a bibliography, measured: 10 of 20 sources became complete records with RIS and BibTeX in 8 seconds. Only one of the other ten was stopped by a bot defence — five pages answered in full and declared no citation data. Mit deutscher Fassung.

entry.title: This site runs an MCP server. Measured: it is smaller than the file it competes with
entry.summary: An MCP endpoint that turns any URL into a reference with RIS and BibTeX — or names the paywall that stopped it. Seven complete records from ten sources in 4.8 s.

entry.title: The sources a machine cannot cite for you — and how to cite them anyway
entry.summary: Ten of twenty sources came back uncited. Three different causes, three different responses — and only one is solved by opening the page in a browser. How to tell them apart, and how to cite a web source that declares nothing about itself.

entry.title: Rechnen Sie eine Zahl nach — am liebsten die, die falsch ist
entry.summary: Der nuetzlichste Beitrag zu diesem Projekt ist eine Gegenmessung, die etwas anderes ergibt. Wo die veroeffentlichten Zahlen am wahrscheinlichsten wackeln, steht hier benannt — samt Rohdaten, offenen Aufgaben und der Anbindung fuer KI-Agenten.

entry.title: Installing a browser extension without a click, and removing it again
entry.summary: Four routes measured on 3 August 2026. Firefox's own Marionette channel installs and uninstalls a signed store extension headless in 9.4 seconds with zero input events and no visible window. The click route took 179.4 seconds and installed nothing while reporting success at every step.

entry.title: German-language scholarly platforms measured: four read, seven handed back
entry.summary: Eleven platforms a student at a German-speaking university actually cites — repositories, the National Library, German publishers, case law, official statistics. Four return a complete record; for the other seven this page names the reason: wall, missing declaration, or unreachable. Deutsche Fassung auf derselben Seite.

entry.title: For AI agents: citations without a browser, and the step that needs one
entry.summary: An MCP endpoint that turns a URL into a citation record with RIS and BibTeX — no account, no key — plus the measured rule for the sources it hands back, and whether your agent can drive the capture extension itself.

entry.title: Can an AI agent use a browser extension? Measured — and the answer has two halves
entry.summary: An agent cannot install a browser extension into a browser it has no access to — no store has an API for that, and inline install was removed years ago. On a machine it does reach, it can: the signed store build goes into the real profile headless in 4.1 s over Firefox's Marionette channel. What it still cannot do is see the page afterwards without a real input event. Measured, including the flag that fails silently.

entry.title: An agent can cite eight of twelve sources. The useful part is knowing which four it cannot
entry.summary: Given a mixed reading list, an MCP endpoint turned 8 of 12 sources into complete citations with RIS records in 13 seconds. The other four are blocked to any server-side reader — and saying so precisely is worth more than guessing. Mit deutscher Fassung.

entry.title: Which page-saving extensions actually run on Firefox for Android?
entry.summary: 248 Firefox extensions for saving or capturing a page, checked against the add-ons API on 2 August 2026. 60 declare Android support — including SingleFile with 85,724 users. Declaration is not function, and that distinction is where most claims fall apart.

entry.title: Web citations that vanish: what happens to a source after you cite it
entry.summary: 150 web sources from reference lists, checked: 19.3% are gone, and the newest archived copy is a median of 603 days old. What that means for a thesis, and how to secure a source in the moment you cite it. Mit deutscher Fassung.

entry.title: Pages that are gone before you need them: eight moments in a degree
entry.summary: Submission receipts, course rooms after the semester ends, the version of an examination regulation that applied when you enrolled: eight situations in a degree where a screen matters later and is no longer there. With what to keep, what not to keep, and why. Mit deutscher Fassung.

entry.title: Measured against Citoid on random samples: same coverage, nothing invented
entry.summary: Citation extraction measured against Wikimedia Citoid on random samples: same coverage, 100 % accuracy against its 79 %, and the selection bias that skewed the first run.

entry.title: Webpage to PDF for OCR: how much text survives? A measured test
entry.summary: A full-page screenshot PDF run through Tesseract and compared against the original article text. 92.6% of the vocabulary survives, and the resolution threshold sits between 72 and 110 dpi. Numbers, method and commands to reproduce it.

entry.title: Six things went wrong building software with an AI assistant in one day
entry.summary: A single day of AI-assisted development, logged honestly: a wrong assumption about browser engines, a false claim that nearly got published, 22 local paths one commit away from a public repo, and three more. What caught each one — and what would not have.

entry.title: Print to PDF or capture the screen? The same page measured both ways
entry.summary: Firefox can already save a page as PDF. So when is a screenshot capture worth it? The same article through both routes: 26 pages against one, 9 sentences cut by page breaks, and a text layer that print keeps and capture loses.

entry.title: Does your PDF extension upload the page? How to check it yourself
entry.summary: Browser extensions declare what they may access. Here is how to read that yourself in 30 seconds, what the current PDF extensions request as of 1 August 2026 — and why a permission is not proof of behaviour.

entry.title: An extension is only as dangerous as its permissions allow
entry.summary: A year ago Mozilla warned that add-on developer accounts were being phished. That is why permissions matter more than trust: they decide what a compromised extension could do. A practical way to judge the risk before installing.
